---
title: "Why I publish my courses in HTML rather than PDF"
description: "An HTML course reads on a phone, can be searched, zoomed and made accessible. The PDF stays available for offline reading."
date: 2026-09-18
categories: [teaching, tools]
---

My lectures have been written in LaTeX for years, and handed out as PDF. This site now publishes them as
**HTML**, session by session, with the PDF still available next to them. Here is why.

## A PDF assumes a large screen

A PDF of slides is made to be projected. On a phone — the screen most of my students actually have — it
forces you to zoom, to drag the page around, to lose the line you were reading. HTML adapts to the width
at hand: text reflows, and the browser's zoom really does enlarge the text.

## What HTML brings

- **Search.** The site's search engine indexes the text of every session: looking for "coupling" leads
  straight to the slide that discusses it.
- **Accessibility.** Every figure carries a description, contrasts are checked on every change, and the
  keyboard is enough to go through everything. A PDF is rarely accessible by accident.
- **Corrections.** Fixing a typo means editing the source and publishing again: no stale version keeps
  circulating.

## What is not lost

The PDF is still produced automatically from the same sources, and downloads from the course page as well as
from the title slide. Reading offline — in a lecture hall without network, or on the bus — remains possible.

## How it works

The LaTeX sources are not rewritten: a script converts them into slides, box by box and figure by figure,
and reports whatever it cannot translate instead of dropping it. Figures become SVG files that follow the
colour of the text, so they stay readable in dark mode and in projection. All of it is replayed on every
change, and the site refuses to publish a page that no longer matches its sources.

The course *Architectures Logicielles Modernes* opens the series, session after session.
